library(jsonlite)

read_json_file <- function (arg0_path) {
  txt <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  fromJSON(paste(txt, collapse = "\n"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json_file("vietnam_laos_cambodia_after_1975.json5")

clean_text <- function (arg0_s) {
  s <- gsub("&", "and", as.character(arg0_s), fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("_", " ", s, fixed = TRUE)
  trimws(s)
}

fmt_yr <- function (arg0_y) {
  y <- as.numeric(arg0_y)
  if (y < 0) return(paste0(abs(round(y)), "BC"))
  return(paste0(round(y), "AD"))
}

# Abstract

Eastern Indochina encompasses 765.511 km² of continental mainland territory across Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia, structured into 9.525 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells. Following three decades of destructive anti-colonial and civil warfare that concluded in 1975, the region underwent profound demographic, political and economic reorganisations. The reunification of Vietnam under the Socialist Republic in 1976, the establishment of the Lao People's Democratic Republic in December 1975 and the catastrophic four-year reign of Democratic Kampuchea from April 1975 to January 1979 radically reshaped settlement hierarchies, family structures and regional population distributions.

Reconstructed across eight administrative and physiographic macro-divisions from 1975 to 2026 under MANDALA, the aggregate regional population expanded from 57,50M in 1975 to 62,50M in 1979, 77,10M in 1989, 93,20M in 1999, 105,40M in 2009, 118,90M in 2019 and 126,25M by 2025. This long-term growth raised aggregate population density from 75,11 persons per km² in 1975 to 164,92 persons per km² in 2025. Across this half-century epoch, the demographic regime shifted from post-war pronatalist reproduction marked by high infant mortality toward advanced demographic transition characterised by rapid fertility contraction, expanding life expectancy and metropolitan agglomeration.

Demographic mass remains intensely concentrated in the major alluvial deltas and industrial corridors. In 2025, the Red River Delta accommodated 23,99M inhabitants (19,0% of the regional total across 32.533 km²; 737,33 persons per km²), anchored by Hanoi and Haiphong. The Southeast province centered on Ho Chi Minh City supported 18,94M residents (15,0% across 25.423 km²; 744,90 persons per km²), forming the primary industrial engine of mainland Southeast Asia. The Mekong River Delta housed 17,68M people (14,0% across 41.100 km²; 430,05 persons per km²), functioning as an intensive wet-rice agrarian core. The North and South Central Coast supported 21,46M inhabitants (17,0% across 107.840 km²; 199,02 persons per km²), while the Northern Midlands and Mountains held 12,62M (10,0% across 93.375 km²; 135,21 persons per km²). The Central Highlands sustained 6,31M residents (5,0% across 55.328 km²; 114,09 persons per km²), transformed by post-1975 planned transmigration and commercial coffee cultivation. Cambodia expanded from 8,05M in 1975 (with severe demographic deficit under the Khmer Rouge) to 17,68M in 2025 (14,0% across 180.174 km²; 98,10 persons per km²). Landlocked Laos expanded from 3,45M in 1975 to 7,58M in 2025 (6,0% across 229.738 km²; 32,97 persons per km²).

This historical demographic study combines 10.635 georeferenced settlement series with decennial population censuses, historical registers and remote sensing inventories. By subtracting nucleated city populations from dasymetrically distributed rural cultivators across environmental suitability grids, the reconstruction captures the spatial balance between rural peasant communities and accelerating metropolitan agglomeration.

# Background

## Post-War Geopolitics and State Reconstruction (1975 to 1979)

The year 1975 marked a decisive geopolitical watershed across eastern Indochina. In April 1975, the fall of Saigon brought the formal conclusion of the Second Indochina War, leading to the administrative reunification of North and South Vietnam into the Socialist Republic of Vietnam in July 1976. Concurrently in Cambodia, the capture of Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975 installed the radical agrarian regime of Democratic Kampuchea led by Pol Pot, which initiated the immediate and forced evacuation of more than two million urban residents into rural labour communes [@Jones2016Cambodia; @Walque2004Long]. In Laos, the abdication of King Savang Vatthana in December 1975 established the Lao People's Democratic Republic under the Lao People's Revolutionary Party.

The immediate post-1975 period witnessed severe demographic dislocations. In Cambodia, the systematic purges, forced agrarian labour, starvation and executions carried out by Democratic Kampuchea eliminated between 1,50M and 2,00M citizens between 1975 and 1979 [@Walque2005Selective; @Heuveline2007Phoenix]. Demographic reconstructions demonstrate pronounced selective mortality: men and educated urbanites suffered disproportionate mortality, while female-headed households confronted severe social disruption and forced communal labour [@Walque2005Selective; @Rashid2023Gender]. Tuol Sleng (S-21) in Phnom Penh and provincial interrogation facilities operated as bureaucratic nodes of incarceration and execution, while urban civil institutions were dismantled [@Jones2023Cambodia; @Manning2014Cambodia]. Post-conflict justice initiatives and documentation efforts have analysed the institutional architecture of these atrocities and their long-term psychological impacts on survivors [@Lee2022Dealing; @Manning2014Cambodia].

The Vietnamese military intervention of December 1978 to January 1979 overthrew Democratic Kampuchea, installing the People's Republic of Kampuchea in Phnom Penh. Concurrently, escalating regional geopolitical frictions culminated in the Sino-Vietnamese border conflict of February 1979, which caused extensive infrastructural destruction across northern Vietnamese border provinces including Lang Son, Cao Bang and Lao Cai. These overlapping conflicts generated enormous refugee outflows. Hundreds of thousands of ethnic Chinese (*Hoa*) and southern Vietnamese fled by sea, while Cambodian refugees established massive border encampments along the Thai frontier, followed by gradual repatriation and demographic reconstitution [@Walque2006Socio; @Heuveline2007Phoenix].

## Agrarian Collectivisation and New Economic Zones

Following reunification, the Vietnamese state attempted to impose northern-style socialist agrarian institutions onto southern agriculture. The Second Five-Year Plan (1976-1980) mandated the collectivisation of the Mekong Delta and Southeast regions into agricultural production collectives (*tập đoàn sản xuất*). Simultaneously, the state initiated ambitious population redistribution programmes known as New Economic Zones (*Kinh tế mới*). Hundreds of thousands of urban residents from Ho Chi Minh City, alongside land-poor peasant households from the densely populated Red River Delta, were resettled into the Central Highlands (*Tây Nguyên*) and peripheral upland districts of the Northern Midlands, altering regional population balances and household living conditions [@Phan2014Internal; @Vo2024Retracted]. Simultaneously, early postwar demographic surveys and census returns recorded high rural fertility alongside universal literacy campaigns [@Fraser1993Vietnam].

These state-directed migrations sought three objectives: relieving acute urban unemployment, expanding national food production through frontier reclamation and securing strategic upland borders. However, inadequate agricultural infrastructure, malaria epidemics and poor soil management hampered early productivity. In Laos, the government similarly introduced agricultural cooperatives (*sahakhan*), though resistance from lowland Lao peasantry and upland ethnic groups led to the suspension of forced collectivisation by 1979. Micro-demographic fieldwork in upland agricultural communities reveals how subsistence rice-farming households navigated severe childhood mortality and labour shortages during this period [@Tomita2015Household].

## Market Reform and Macroeconomic Transition (Doi Moi and Chintanakan Mai)

Severe agricultural shortfalls, hyperinflation exceeding 700% and the reduction of Soviet economic assistance forced systemic structural adjustments during the mid-1980s. The Sixth National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam in December 1986 adopted the policy of *Đổi Mới* (renovation), establishing a socialist-oriented market economy. Agricultural reforms proved decisive: Directive 100 (1981) and Politburo Resolution 10 (1988) dismantled collective farming, granting long-term land-use rights directly to peasant households. Agricultural productivity expanded rapidly; within two years, Vietnam transitioned from a food-deficit country into the second largest global exporter of rice, initiating structural declines in rural fertility as household investment shifted toward education [@Fraser1993Vietnam; @Phan2014Internal].

In Laos, the Fourth Party Congress in 1986 launched *Chintanakan Mai* (New Economic Mechanism), decentralising economic planning, legalising private trade and liberalising foreign exchange. In Cambodia, the withdrawal of Vietnamese military forces between 1989 and 1991 facilitated the Paris Peace Accords of October 1991. The subsequent deployment of the United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC) in 1992-1993 culminated in national democratic elections, repatriation of refugees and the stabilisation of civilian governance, paving the way for the benchmark 1998 General Population Census [@Huguet2000Results; @Walque2004Long].

## Urbanisation, Industrialisation and Demographic Transition

From the 1990s onward, eastern Indochina experienced accelerated industrialisation driven by domestic market liberalisation and foreign direct investment. Export-oriented manufacturing clusters expanded rapidly around Ho Chi Minh City, Binh Duong, Dong Nai, Hanoi, Bac Ninh and Haiphong. Millions of rural migrants moved toward urban centres, shifting the regional balance between countryside and metropolis.

Concurrently, investments in public health and urban services improved living conditions across the region. In Cambodia, post-conflict reconstruction of municipal infrastructure and the expansion of health insurance coverage significantly enhanced antenatal care utilisation, even as urban poor communities in informal settlements faced persistent challenges in household food security [@Um2024Effect; @Boonyabancha2019Urban]. Peri-urban livestock keeping and informal farming provided vital subsistence for peri-urban households adapting to rapid city expansion around Phnom Penh [@Strom2017Urban]. Demographic transition accompanied economic modernisation: total fertility rates in Vietnam dropped from 5,60 births per woman in 1979 to 2,09 by 2009 and 1,95 by 2025, mirroring broader epidemiologic and health transitions observed across developing economies [@Bawah2016Evolving]. Concurrently, institutional modernisation transformed healthcare delivery, leading to dramatic rises in institutional births and caesarean section rates across both urban and rural provinces [@Loenzien2019Magnitude].

However, rapid fertility contraction coincided with persistent son preference, resulting in elevated sex ratios at birth across subnational regions, particularly in the northern deltas, where educational expansion and birth-order dynamics influenced reproductive choices [@F2021Ratio; @Hasegawa2025Evolution]. Longitudinal settlement baselines demonstrate deep structural continuity in municipal site locations across the Mekong basin, where modern commercial cities occupy historical administrative nodes documented in regional archaeological gazetteers, such as the Thailand FADGIS database, Harvard Published Excavations Atlas and NUSARC surveys.

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To model demographic distributions across 765.511 km² of mainland territory, the MANDALA spatial engine discretises eastern Indochina into 9.525 active 5-arcminute grid cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes). Each terrestrial cell is evaluated against environmental and infrastructural covariates:
- Fluvial distance decay: proximity to the Red River, Mekong, Tonle Sap basin and coastal river mouths, with density weightings reflecting irrigation access.
- Floodplain geomasking: continuous surface rasters capturing alluvial soils, deltaic irrigation networks and seasonal flood regimes.
- Topographic slope: penalising rugged terrain along the Annamite Range (*Dãy Trường Sơn*) and northern karst highlands while prioritising flat alluvial plains and coastal bluffs.
- Transport connectivity: proximity to national arterial corridors including Highway 1, the Trans-Mekong highway and coastal ports.

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To eliminate double counting between nucleated urban centres and rural agricultural populations, 10.635 catalogued settlements with continuous chronological population series are georeferenced to WGS84 coordinates. At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements within each sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The remaining rural population is dasymetrically distributed across non-settled pixels in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A boundary feathering filter smoothes density transitions across internal provincial and national borders, preventing abrupt step discontinuities along watershed divides.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every sub-regional estimate carries an explicit symmetric uncertainty bound (+/- 3,0% to +/- 6,0% across benchmark years). The regional total of 57,50M in 1975 is bounded between 55,78M and 59,22M inhabitants, while the 2025 total of 126,25M is bounded between 122,46M and 130,04M. This interval accommodates variances in post-war registration coverage, unregistered rural-to-urban labour migration and census enumeration discrepancies.

Table \ref{tab:subregions} documents the eight sub-regions, land areas, benchmark populations and 2025 population densities.

```{r tbl-subregions, results='asis'}
sub_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  a <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p_1975 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1975"]])
  p_1979 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1979"]])
  p_1989 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1989"]])
  p_1999 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1999"]])
  p_2009 <- as.numeric(r$population[["2009"]])
  p_2019 <- as.numeric(r$population[["2019"]])
  p_2025 <- as.numeric(r$population[["2025"]])
  dens_2025 <- p_2025 / a
  data.frame(
    Region = if (!is.null(reg_short[[rk]])) reg_short[[rk]] else clean_text(r$name),
    Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(a, 0L), " (", viscount_fmt_number(a / tot_area * 100, 1L), "%)"),
    P1975 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1975),
    P1979 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1979),
    P1989 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1989),
    P1999 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1999),
    P2009 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_2009),
    P2019 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_2019),
    P2025 = viscount_fmt_pop(p_2025),
    Density2025 = viscount_fmt_number(dens_2025, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sub <- do.call(rbind, sub_rows)
df_tot <- data.frame(
  Region = "Regional Total",
  Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(tot_area, 0L), " (100%)"),
  P1975 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1975),
  P1979 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1979"]]),
  P1989 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1989"]]),
  P1999 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1999"]]),
  P2009 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["2009"]]),
  P2019 = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["2019"]]),
  P2025 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_2025),
  Density2025 = viscount_fmt_number(tot_2025 / tot_area, 2L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_sub <- rbind(df_sub, df_tot)
viscount_table(
  df_sub,
  "Sub-regional land area, benchmark populations and 2025 density across Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia.",
  c("Sub-Region", "Area km² (Share)", "1975", "1979", "1989", "1999", "2009", "2019", "2025", "2025 Density"),
  list(label = "tab:subregions", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Testing and Validation

## Multi-Decadal Census Ingestion and Inter-Censal Harmonisation

The historical demographic baseline reconciles official decennial and quinquennial national censuses conducted across the three sovereign nations:
- Vietnam: 1979 National Population Census (52,74M), 1989 Census (64,41M), 1999 Census (76,32M), 2009 Census (85,85M) and 2019 Census (96,21M), published by the General Statistics Office in Hanoi.
- Cambodia: 1980 administrative headcounts under the People's Republic of Kampuchea, 1998 General Population Census (11,44M), 2008 Census (13,40M) and 2019 Census (15,55M), published by the National Institute of Statistics in Phnom Penh.
- Laos: 1985 First Population Census (3,58M), 1995 Census (4,57M), 2005 Census (5,62M) and 2015 Census (6,49M), published by the Lao Statistics Bureau in Vientiane.

Because provincial and district boundaries changed frequently through administrative mergers and splits, sub-regional boundaries are standardised using modern 2026 GIS polygons, back-projecting historical district-level population series into stable geographical units.

## Remote Sensing of Urban Footprints and Night-Time Lights

To validate urban settlement growth independent of administrative reclassifications, multi-temporal remote sensing datasets were cross-referenced against catalogued settlement populations. Landsat and Sentinel-2 satellite imagery spanning from 1984 to 2025 track the spatial expansion of built-up impervious surfaces across the Red River Delta and the Ho Chi Minh City metropolitan fringe.

Additionally, intercalibrated night-time light series from DMSP-OLS (1992-2013) and VIIRS Day-Night Band (2012-2025) provide continuous radiometric validation of economic concentration and electrification. The expansion of high-radiance urban cores closely correlates with population growth in secondary cities such as Da Nang, Can Tho, Bien Hoa, Siem Reap and Savannakhet.

## Hydrological Constraints and Floodplain Settlement Stability

Sedimentation and hydrological dynamics in the Mekong and Red River basins establish natural boundaries for urban expansion. Coring profiles and flood hazard mapping demonstrate that settlements in the lower Mekong Delta must manage annual inundation and seasonal saltwater intrusion. The historical durability of dyke networks in the Red River Delta has preserved high settlement continuity across centuries, insulating dense rural communes against seasonal flooding.

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The MANDALA source ledger was compiled through four successive ingestion waves:
- Wave 1: Official censuses and national statistical registries, yielding 6.594 georeferenced settlements.
- Wave 2: Archival monographs, provincial gazetteers and institutional catalogues, adding 2.871 settlements.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation-year audits, adding 1.170 localities.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap hunting and homonym audits across all eight sub-regions, confirming complete spatial coverage with zero unaccounted settlements (marginal gain 0,0%).

In total, 11.435 candidate settlements were audited: 10.635 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements and 800 were excluded (predominantly duplicate survey aliases within a 2,2 km spatial buffer or non-habitation administrative points).

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Benchmark Analysis

The demographic history of eastern Indochina between 1975 and 2026 exhibits sustained expansion driven by post-war demographic recovery, agrarian reforms and metropolitan industrialisation (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_vietnam_laos_cambodia_after_1975_demography.png",
  "Long-term demographic trajectory of Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia (1975 to 2026), showing benchmark population growth across eight sub-regions, post-war recovery and metropolitan agglomeration.",
  "fig:trajectory"
)
```

```{r tbl-benchmarks, results='asis'}
bm_years <- c("1975", "1979", "1989", "1999", "2009", "2019", "2025")
bm_rows <- lapply(bm_years, function (yk) {
  tot_pop <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[yk]])
  rrd <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$vlc_vn_rrd$population[[yk]])
  nmt <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$vlc_vn_north_mt$population[[yk]])
  cen <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$vlc_vn_central$population[[yk]])
  hig <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$vlc_vn_highlands$population[[yk]])
  se <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$vlc_vn_southeast$population[[yk]])
  mek <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$vlc_vn_mekong$population[[yk]])
  cam <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$vlc_cambodia$population[[yk]])
  lao <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$vlc_laos$population[[yk]])
  dens <- tot_pop / tot_area
  data.frame(
    Benchmark = yk,
    TotalPop = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_pop),
    Density = viscount_fmt_number(dens, 2L),
    RedRiver = viscount_fmt_pop(rrd),
    Southeast = viscount_fmt_pop(se),
    CentralCoast = viscount_fmt_pop(cen),
    MekongDelta = viscount_fmt_pop(mek),
    Cambodia = viscount_fmt_pop(cam),
    Laos = viscount_fmt_pop(lao),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_bm <- do.call(rbind, bm_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_bm,
  "Benchmark population totals and sub-regional distribution across Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia (1975 to 2026).",
  c("Benchmark", "Regional Pop", "Density", "Red River", "Southeast", "Central Coast", "Mekong Delta", "Cambodia", "Laos"),
  list(label = "tab:benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Five Historical Demographic Epochs

### Post-War Turmoil, Autarky and Collectivisation (1975 to 1986)

The first post-war decade was defined by deep institutional disruption, severe poverty and administrative command economics. Regional population rose from 57,50M in 1975 to 62,50M in 1979 and 72,50M by 1986. While fertility remained high in rural Vietnam and Laos (crude birth rates exceeding 35 per 1.000), Cambodia suffered massive demographic suppression under the Khmer Rouge (1975-1979), losing between a fifth and a quarter of its population to state-directed violence, famine and disease [@Jones2016Cambodia; @Walque2005Selective]. Following the January 1979 overthrow of the regime, Cambodia experienced a compensatory marriage and birth rebound, characterised by a phoenix population dynamic where surviving cohorts remarried rapidly despite profound sex ratio imbalances and adult male deficits [@Walque2006Socio; @Heuveline2007Phoenix].

In Vietnam, state efforts to collectivise agriculture in the south triggered production declines and food rationing. The creation of New Economic Zones moved over 1,30M people into upland provinces, establishing new rural settlements in Tay Nguyen and the northern hills. Simultaneously, hundreds of thousands fled abroad as refugees, moderating net population growth across southern coastal districts. Industrial plants suffered from shortages of raw materials and spare parts, leaving urban workers dependent on subsidised state distribution networks.

### Early Market Transition and Agricultural De-Collectivisation (1986 to 1999)

The introduction of *Đổi Mới* in Vietnam (December 1986) and *Chintanakan Mai* in Laos (1986) marked the transition to household-based agrarian production and market pricing. Regional population grew from 72,50M in 1986 to 77,10M in 1989 and 93,20M by 1999. In Vietnam, Resolution 10 restored peasant family farming, sparking rapid productivity gains in the Red River and Mekong deltas, while inter-censal data documented rising literacy and steady declines in completed family size [@Fraser1993Vietnam]. Internal migration accelerated as rural labourers moved toward urban periphery zones and upland frontier settlements [@Phan2014Internal; @Vo2024Retracted]. In northern Laos, village-level demographic studies recorded gradual reductions in early childhood mortality as basic immunisation and rural health posts took root [@Tomita2015Household]. In Cambodia, the 1998 census recorded a national population of 11,44M, confirming substantial demographic recovery alongside a distinctive pyramid distorted by Khmer Rouge mortality deficits [@Huguet2000Results].

In the Central Highlands, the liberalisation of commercial agriculture triggered a coffee boom. Spontaneous migration of millions of Kinh peasant settlers from northern provinces transformed Dac Lac, Gia Lai and Lam Dong into densely settled cash-crop zones, altering the ethnic and ecological composition of the highlands. In Cambodia, the 1991 Paris Peace Accords and 1993 elections restored constitutional governance, encouraging the return of 370k refugees from Thai border camps and stabilising national population growth at 2,5% annually. Re-established provincial administrative bodies began repairing irrigation canals and rural road networks.

### Industrial Acceleration and Global Integration (1999 to 2009)

Between 1999 and 2009, regional population expanded from 93,20M to 105,40M. This decade witnessed the rapid emergence of eastern Indochina as an international manufacturing hub. Vietnam's bilateral trade agreement with the United States in 2000 and accession to the World Trade Organisation in 2007 spurred foreign direct investment in electronics, garments and footwear.

Industrial corridors expanded around Ho Chi Minh City (Binh Duong, Dong Nai and Ba Ria-Vung Tau) and Hanoi (Bac Ninh, Vinh Phuc and Hung Yen). Concurrently, national fertility fell sharply: Vietnam attained replacement-level fertility (2,03 births per woman) by 2006, though Bayesian demographic reconstructions show a simultaneous divergence in subnational sex ratios at birth in northern coastal provinces [@F2021Ratio]. Long-term assessments of Cambodian educational cohorts revealed enduring deficits in human capital accumulation attributable to childhood trauma during the 1970s [@Walque2004Long], while urban growth stimulated peri-urban agricultural diversification [@Strom2017Urban]. In Cambodia, garment manufacturing and international tourism centred on Siem Reap drove rapid urban growth in Phnom Penh, while Laos expanded mineral extraction and hydropower generation along the Mekong tributaries.

### Metropolitan Concentration and Regional Infrastructure Corridors (2009 to 2019)

From 2009 to 2019, regional population rose from 105,40M to 118,90M. Urban agglomerations absorbed the majority of demographic growth, while rural populations in peripheral districts stagnated or contracted due to out-migration. Greater Ho Chi Minh City expanded into a contiguous mega-urban region exceeding 14M residents, while Greater Hanoi reached 8,2M.

Major transport infrastructure projects, including expressways, deep-water ports at Cai Mep and Lach Huyen and regional air hubs, accelerated cross-border trade. In Laos, the initiation of the Boten-Vientiane railway connected landlocked interior valleys to international rail corridors. Cambodia experienced rapid real estate investment and coastal expansion in Sihanoukville, while Phnom Penh diversified into financial services and light manufacturing.

### Contemporary Deceleration, Ageing and Secondary City Growth (2019 to 2026)

In the contemporary period from 2019 to 2026, regional population expanded from 118,90M to 126,25M. The rate of natural increase declined significantly, dropping below 1,0% annually in Vietnam. Urban fertility in Ho Chi Minh City and the Red River Delta fell below 1,5 births per woman. Projections based on compositional age-structure modelling indicate that Vietnam will experience rapid population ageing over the coming decade, with the proportion of elderly citizens expanding sharply as working-age cohorts peak [@Wei2019Predicting]. Simultaneously, fertility behaviours continue to reflect evolving gender norms and educational attainment, where higher compulsory schooling interacts with birth-order parity to shape family composition [@Hasegawa2025Evolution].

Government policy increasingly prioritised secondary and tertiary urban centres to relieve infrastructure congestion in the primary metropolises. Cities such as Da Nang, Can Tho, Hai Phong, Hue, Battambang and Vientiane developed specialised logistics, technology and service sectors. The COVID-19 pandemic temporarily disrupted urban-to-rural migration streams in 2020-2021, prompting short-term reverse migration before urban industrial employment rebounded in 2022-2026.

## Urban Hierarchy and Settlement Systems

Table \ref{tab:leading_settlements} presents the leading fifteen catalogued settlements across Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia ordered by peak population.

```{r tbl-leading-settlements, results='asis'}
set_list <- unname(set_data)
sett_peaks <- vapply(set_list, function (s) {
  if (is.null(s$population) || length(s$population) == 0) return(0)
  max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
}, numeric(1))

ord <- order(sett_peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_sett <- set_list[ord]

top_rows <- lapply(head(top_sett, 15), function (s) {
  p_max <- max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
  p_2025 <- if (!is.null(s$population[["2025"]])) as.numeric(s$population[["2025"]]) else "-"
  lat <- as.numeric(s$coords[[1]])
  lon <- as.numeric(s$coords[[2]])
  coord_str <- paste0(viscount_fmt_number(abs(lat), 2L), if (lat >= 0) " N" else " S", ", ",
                      viscount_fmt_number(abs(lon), 2L), if (lon >= 0) " E" else " W")
  reg_lbl <- if (!is.null(reg_short[[s$region_id]])) reg_short[[s$region_id]] else clean_text(s$region)
  data.frame(
    Name = clean_text(s$name),
    SubRegion = reg_lbl,
    Coordinates = coord_str,
    PeakPop = viscount_fmt_pop(p_max),
    P2025 = if (is.numeric(p_2025)) viscount_fmt_pop(p_2025) else "-",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_top <- do.call(rbind, top_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_top,
  "Leading fifteen modern settlements across Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia, showing coordinates, peak population and 2025 population.",
  c("Settlement Name", "Sub-Region", "Coordinates", "Peak Pop", "2025 Pop"),
  list(label = "tab:leading_settlements", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

The regional urban system conforms to a structured multi-tiered hierarchy:
1. Primary megacities (> 5M inhabitants): Ho Chi Minh City (14,56M peak, 14,56M in 2025) and Hanoi (8,72M in 2025). These dual metropolitan poles coordinate national finance, political administration, corporate headquarters and higher education.
2. Major regional metropolises (1M to 5M inhabitants): Can Tho (3,12M in 2025) commanding the Mekong Delta, Da Nang (2,82M in 2025) anchoring the central coast, Hai Phong (2,73M in 2025) serving as northern maritime gateway, Phnom Penh (1,70M in 2025) functioning as Cambodia's national capital, Hue (1,38M peak), Bien Hoa (1,32M in 2025) and Vientiane (1,00M peak) serving as the capital of Laos.
3. Secondary provincial centres (200k to 1M inhabitants): Khanh Hoa (Nha Trang, 1,28M), Binh Thuan (Phan Thiet, 1,28M), Ben Tre (1,25M), Ca Mau (1,24M), Soc Trang (1,23M), Tay Ninh (1,22M), Ba Ria-Vung Tau (1,21M), Lam Dong (Da Lat, 1,20M), Siem Reap (160k) and Battambang (140k).
4. Tertiary district towns and rural market centres (< 200k inhabitants): thousands of district capitals (*thị trấn*), river ports and border trading gates distributed throughout the interior provinces.

# Limitations

Historical demographic analysis across eastern Indochina is subject to distinct methodological constraints:
1. Khmer Rouge mortality variances and demographic loss: the absence of administrative records during Democratic Kampuchea (1975-1979) creates uncertainty regarding excess mortality estimates, which range between 1,2M and 2,2M across scholarly sources [@Walque2005Selective; @Heuveline2007Phoenix; @Jones2023Cambodia]. Disentangling direct execution from indirect starvation and disease remains methodologically challenging across provincial sectors.
2. Household survey sampling and informal migration: the household registration system in Vietnam (*hộ khẩu*) historically led to undercounting of seasonal and informal migrant workers residing in urban periphery districts without permanent registration [@Vo2024Retracted]. In Cambodia, specialised questioning techniques and indirect survey designs highlight the difficulty of measuring sensitive socio-economic and resource-use behaviours among rural households [@Davis2019Understand].
3. Administrative boundary reclassifications: frequent splits, mergers and elevation of rural communes into wards or towns complicate longitudinal comparisons of individual settlement sizes over time.
4. Remote upland enumeration: linguistic diversity and rugged mountainous topography in the northern highlands and Annamite Range presented logistical challenges for census enumeration teams, particularly during early post-war decades.

# Conclusion

Between 1975 and 2026, Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia achieved remarkable demographic growth and structural transformation, expanding from 57,50M to 126,25M inhabitants across 765.511 km² of territory. The initial post-war epoch was marked by political turmoil, radical social engineering, Khmer Rouge genocide and refugee displacement. Subsequent market-oriented policy shifts—*Đổi Mới* in Vietnam, *Chintanakan Mai* in Laos and post-UNTAC reconstruction in Cambodia—unlocked rapid agricultural productivity and industrial expansion.

This transformation restructured the human geography of the region. Dense deltaic farming populations in the Red River and Mekong deltas were complemented by the explosive emergence of metropolitan manufacturing agglomerations around Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi. As eastern Indochina enters the second quarter of the twenty-first century, moderating fertility, population ageing and metropolitan decentralisation define the next frontier of regional demographic evolution.

# Appendix

The MANDALA source ledger audited 11.435 candidate settlements across eastern Indochina, resulting in 10.635 accepted catalogued localities and 800 exclusions. Table \ref{tab:saturation} summarises the four-wave asymptotic saturation audit demonstrating regional enumeration coverage.

```{r tbl-saturation, results='asis'}
sat_waves <- led_data$saturation_audit$waves
sat_rows <- lapply(sat_waves, function (w) {
  data.frame(
    Wave = paste0("Wave ", w$wave),
    SourceClass = clean_text(w$source_class),
    PriorTotal = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$prior_cumulative_included), 0L),
    NewlyIncluded = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$newly_included), 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sat <- do.call(rbind, sat_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_sat,
  "Four-wave asymptotic saturation audit of catalogued settlements across Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia.",
  c("Ingestion Wave", "Source Category", "Prior Cumulative", "Newly Included"),
  list(label = "tab:saturation", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```
